editorialPurpose: Explain how extracellular ice, water redistribution and complementary cryoprotectants let a wood frog survive a reversible freeze.

narrationPlan.voiceDirection: Controlled wonder: open with quiet disbelief, become precise during the mechanism, and land the final distinction without triumphal exaggeration.

narrativeStructure.label: Reversible cardiac arrest
narrativeStructure.purpose: Create immediate disbelief without implying death or resurrection.

narrativeStructure.label: Extracellular freeze
narrativeStructure.purpose: Establish substantial body-water freezing without depicting uniform intracellular ice.

narrativeStructure.label: Water leaves the cells
narrativeStructure.purpose: Show how extracellular ice, dehydration and extra-organ sequestration reduce dangerous ice inside tissues and cells.

narrativeStructure.label: Two defenses, different timing
narrativeStructure.purpose: Distinguish freeze-triggered glucose mobilization from urea accumulated before freezing.

narrativeStructure.label: Ordered recovery
narrativeStructure.purpose: Show heart function returning before breathing and hindleg reflexes, then land the controlled-freeze distinction.

segments.text: A wood frog can survive a freeze that stops its heartbeat—then thaw and recover.
Much of its body water can turn to ice, mainly outside its cells.
As extracellular ice grows, water leaves the cells. That dehydration helps keep dangerous ice crystals from forming inside them.
Its liver rapidly releases glucose, while urea has already built up before freezing.
These cryoprotectants limit ice formation and help protect cells through freezing and thawing.
As the frog thaws, its heart starts beating first; breathing and leg reflexes follow. It survived by controlling the freeze—not by staying unfrozen.

storyAngle: Begin with reversible cardiac arrest, correct the “frozen solid” misconception, then reveal the physical and chemical defenses that permit staged recovery.

assetRequirements: Original procedural or vector wood frog model
visualPlan.notes: A flat trace represents measured cardiac arrest, not death. Do not use a hospital death monitor, alarm, resurrection flash or medical-emergency language.
visualPlan.objective: Show a stylized wood frog freezing while a clearly labeled cardiac trace slows and ceases, then briefly preview recovery after thaw.

visualPlan.notes: Do not fill the frog or its cells with a uniform solid-ice texture. This is an explanatory diagram, not a literal scan.
visualPlan.objective: Move from leaf litter into a simplified body view where extracellular and extra-organ ice grows while cells remain visibly unfrozen inside.

visualPlan.notes: Label extracellular space, cell membrane and water movement. Intracellular ice may appear only as a crossed-out danger example, never as the normal survivable state.
visualPlan.objective: Show extracellular ice drawing water out of a cell, controlled cell shrinkage, and water accumulating in extra-organ spaces without showing survivable intracellular crystals.
Use a two-step timeline: urea is already elevated before freezing; after ice nucleation, liver glycogen becomes glucose that travels to tissues before advanced freezing impedes transport.

assetRequirements: Original procedural or vector recovered frog visual
visualPlan.notes: The order is supported, but exact recovery timing varies and must not be implied by an unlabeled stopwatch.
visualPlan.objective: Thaw the extracellular ice, restore the cardiac trace first, then show breathing and a hindleg reflex returning without assigning unsupported exact times.
